note: Guide lines from a helper pattern to al-Jady are modern UFUQ teaching constructions (decision D-4, MODERN_PEDAGOGICAL); no local source attests them as historical methods. Only al-Jady's use for direction finding is historically attested, and it is cited separately as historical context, never as a modern Qibla or navigation algorithm.

relationships.explanation: al-Jady lies close to the north celestial pole, so the point on the horizon directly below it is close to True North. al-Jady is a star cue; True North is a direction on the ground, and they are not the same thing.

historicalContext.text: Arabic anwa literature records al-Jady being used to find direction.

citations.locator: ADR-003: Polaris remains a star cue distinct from terrestrial True North

relationships.explanation: Stand facing True North, the point on the horizon below al-Jady. The Qibla is the shortest way over the Earth to the Kaaba. From this place it is a fixed angle clockwise from True North: turn that many degrees through east, south and west, or equally turn the rest of the way back from north towards the west.

historicalContext.text: Arabic anwa writers tied the qibla to al-Jady for their own lands, for example al-Jady against the right shoulder in Iraq. Such rules belong to their place; away from it the angle must be computed for the observer.

citations.supports: deriving the Qibla bearing from True North by spherical trigonometry
